content: The United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) aim to reduce the global maternal mortality rate to fewer than 70 deaths per 100,000 live births and to eliminate preventable deaths of newborns and children under five years of age in all countries by 2030. Maternal and perinatal death audits and reviews are widely recommended as strategies to reduce maternal and perinatal mortality and to improve the quality of care. These interventions may play a critical role in achieving the SDGs. However, there is uncertainty regarding the most cost-effective approach to conducting these audits and reviews. Options include community-based audits (such as verbal and social autopsies), facility-based audits (such as significant event analysis), or a combination of both approaches (such as confidential enquiries). The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact and cost-effectiveness of various types of death audits and reviews in reducing maternal, perinatal, and child mortality. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, and Embase, up to January 16, 2019. Ongoing studies were identified through ClinicalTrials.gov and the World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. Reference lists of included articles were also reviewed. Eligible studies included cluster-randomized trials, cluster non-randomized trials, controlled before-and-after studies, and interrupted time series studies. These studies needed to involve the review of individual cases of maternal, perinatal, or child deaths, identify avoidable factors, and make recommendations. To be included, studies had to report at least one of the following outcomes: perinatal mortality rate, stillbirth rate, neonatal mortality rate, mortality rate in children under five years of age, or maternal mortality rate. Data collection and analysis followed standard Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care (EPOC) group methodological procedures. Two independent reviewers extracted data, assessed the risk of bias, and evaluated the certainty of the evidence using the GRADE approach. Although a meta-analysis was planned, the included studies were too heterogeneous to allow for meaningful pooling of results. Two cluster-randomized trials were included in the review. Both trials introduced death review and audit as part of a multicomponent intervention and compared this to standard care. The QUARITE study, conducted in hospitals in West Africa, focused on maternal death reviews in settings with very high maternal and perinatal mortality rates. In contrast, the OPERA trial, conducted in maternity units in France, examined perinatal morbidity and mortality conferences (MMCs) in a high-income setting with already low baseline perinatal mortality rates. The OPERA intervention in France began with an outreach visit to brief obstetricians, midwives, and anesthetists on national guidelines for morbidity and mortality case management. This was followed by a series of perinatal MMCs. Half of the intervention units were randomized to receive additional support from a clinical psychologist during these meetings. The OPERA intervention may have little or no effect on overall perinatal mortality (low-certainty evidence). However, its impact on perinatal mortality related to suboptimal care is uncertain (very low-certainty evidence). The intervention probably reduces perinatal morbidity related to suboptimal care (unadjusted odds ratio [OR] 0.62, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.40 to 0.95; 165,353 births; moderate-certainty evidence). The effect of the intervention on stillbirth rate, neonatal mortality, mortality rate in children under five years of age, maternal mortality, or adverse effects was not reported. The QUARITE intervention in West Africa involved training hospital obstetric team leaders using the ALARM (Advances in Labour and Risk Management) course, which included one day of training on conducting maternal death reviews. These leaders returned to their hospitals, established multidisciplinary committees, and began auditing maternal deaths with support from external facilitators. The intervention probably reduces inpatient maternal deaths (adjusted OR 0.85, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.98; 191,167 deliveries; moderate-certainty evidence) and probably reduces inpatient neonatal mortality within 24 hours of birth (adjusted OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.90; moderate-certainty evidence). However, the intervention probably has little or no effect on the inpatient stillbirth rate (moderate-certainty evidence) and may have little or no effect on inpatient neonatal mortality after 24 hours, with the 95% CI including both benefit and harm (low-certainty evidence). The QUARITE intervention probably increases the percentage of women receiving high-quality care (OR 1.87, 95% CI 1.35 to 2.57; moderate-certainty evidence). The effect of the intervention on perinatal mortality, mortality rate in children under five years of age, or adverse effects was not reported. No studies were identified that evaluated child death audits and reviews, community-based death reviews, or the costs associated with these interventions. In conclusion, a complex intervention that includes maternal death audits and reviews, along with the development of local leadership and training, probably reduces inpatient maternal mortality in district hospitals in low-income countries and likely improves the quality of care. Perinatal death audits and reviews, as part of a complex intervention with training, probably improve the quality of care in high-income settings where mortality rates are already very low, as measured by reductions in perinatal morbidity related to suboptimal care. The WHO recommends that maternal and perinatal death reviews be conducted in all hospitals worldwide. However, conducting death reviews in isolation may not be sufficient to achieve the reductions in mortality observed in the QUARITE trial. This review suggests that maternal death audits and reviews may need to be implemented as part of a broader intervention package that includes training for hospital leaders, annual recertification, and quarterly outreach visits by external facilitators for supervision and mentorship. Similar considerations may apply to perinatal and child death reviews. Further operational research is needed to identify the most cost-effective ways to implement maternal, perinatal, and pediatric death reviews in lowand middle-income countries.
